newsitem.title: UK: Upcoming U.S. GDP data weigh on Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: Upcoming U.S. GDP data weigh on Treasuries.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries face a no-win situation from economic growth data this week, analysts said on Thursday.

If the figures are too strong the market may see the Federal Reserve as too relaxed over inflation. But a soft report may only prolong the agony of waiting for what many see as an inevitable rate rise.
For the moment, a tightening at next week's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) gathering is not expected, analysts say.

"Recent data show growth is well in excess of trend," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas in London. "But it really depends on how pre-emptive the Federal Reserve wants to be. A rate rise may be what the market needs."
Fourth quarter GDP, scheduled for Friday at 1330 GMT, was forecast to rise 3.9 percent versus 2.1 percent previously.
The FOMC, the policy arm of the Federal Reserve, meets on February 4 and 5. The federal funds rate is currently at 5.25 percent, and the last move was a cut in rates in January 1996.

Although a high GDP figure could push the T-note/Bund spread through the 100 basis point barrier, the period of Bund outperformance was likely to be limited, analysts said. The spread at 1200 GMT was 95 basis points.
Even though there were expectations of falling interest rates in Europe, they would be just the last gasp of the easing cycle -- and not an indication that European and U.S. economies were decoupled.
France, Germany, Italy and Spain are all being touted as possible candidates for rate cuts, analysts said.
"The broader, whole-of-1997 view of Europe is not one of easing interest rates," said Wattret. "It is unusual for the German and U.S. economies to remain out of sync for a long time."

He said sentiment would turn once there was any sign of growth in Germany. "If the spread were to have sustained a break through 100, it would have already have done it. It may get to 110 but we're looking for narrowing in the second quarter."
Indeed, a rate increase in the U.S. could hasten that prospect, analysts said.
Andrew Davies, bond analyst at the London Bond Broking Company, said Treasuries' recent choppy trading illustrated how much nervousness there was about interest rate policy.
"A rate rise would help," he said. "It would signal a change in direction, and take the suspense out of the equation."
He said he was expecting the Fed to raise the fed funds rate next week by a quarter percentage point.
Davies said Fed chairman Alan Greenspan's recent focus on non-wage elements in employment costs, such as health care, suggested overall wage pressures are on his mind.
"The Fed has to act if there is trouble looming."

He also argued that an interest rate move might be likely if Greenspan was concerned about U.S. equity market levels as he was perceived to be following a question he posed in December about the potential for "irrational exuberence" in markets.
But Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London, said a rise in the U.S. would prompt the outperformance of European bond markets.
He said Bunds could be set to outperform, with the spread heading towards 125 basis points.
The 10-year Bund yield could fall to 5.5 percent, from a current level of 5.78 percent while the comparable U.S. Treasury yields could hit 6.75 percent, he said.
"Even without tomorrow's data, it is obvious that the U.S. economy is growing strongly," he said. "Meanwhile the outlook for Europe is still fairly bleak."
